ANC Money Woes

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Unpaid salaries and party donors shying away from the ANC, is the ruling party on the brink of bankruptcy

Unique Selling Point:
A party mired in fractious factionalism, internal legal battles, organisational problems, the ANC is now contending with a empty coffers. Over a hundred years old and once respected globally, South Africa's rulling has not its employees in three months and disgruntled staff members maintain Luthuli House has not been making contributions to their UIF and provident fund. The insert is analysis of the party's financial status, featuring expert voices, dissatisfied workers and traces the root of the party's money problems.

Summary:
The introduction of the Political Party Funding Bill is forcing parties to open up their books and declare their donors and donations. Whilst many parties, including the ANC, have previously secured handsome donations from private entities and wealthy people, the bill will now reveal these transaction. Without the security of these donations remaining secrecy, parties stand to lose donors who don't wish to be exposed. A combination of financial mismanagement and donors shying away from Luthuli House is proving to problematic for the ruling party.

Press Release:


When President Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Political Party Funding Act into action, he said it was a historic development for transparency and accountability. As the ANC has been dogged by allegations of corruption, dodgy tenders and kick-backs the move was widely welcomed. But once bankrolled by the wealthy and influential, the introduction of the Act now requires parties to disclose all donations over R100,000 and restricts funding sources, raising the question of how the ANC would retain some of its previously controversial benefactors. Incrementally a veil has been lifted on the ruling party’s finances and despite denials that Luthuli House is bankrupt, personnel have been left with unpaid salaries months in a row, growing more desperate and disgruntled by the day. Is South Africa’s ruling party on the brink of financial ruin?
Producers: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje & Siniketiwe Hlanze | Presenter: Bongani Bingwa

Script:


VO - For 37 year old Mandla Qwane, choosing to work for the African National Congress came naturally. The real challenge for him has been keeping the job.

Once known for hosting costly election campaigns and rallies, the ruling party is seemingly a shell of its former self.

Qwane’s anxiety is worsened by the fact that his employer has been unable to afford to pay his salary for the past three months.

The problem began last year when he realised he was no longer receiving his income on time.

SOUND UP - MANDLA QWANE

6:40 When it happened the first time we were all not ready. We were shocked
07:16 That first time Our salaries came in on the 28th if not the 29th of the month .It wasn't much of a worry. And then it happened the following months as well. Which was a bit longer. 07:35 It went to the start of the next month. That's when we realised that there is a bit of a problem. But we were still calm about it because we thought it's something that will be addressed.

VO - Qwane is a member of the Staff Representative Committee, a forum of employees that was initially formed to facilitate negotiations with the ANC.

He says they were told the party is not in a position to pay outstanding salaries of more than 240 staff members nationally.
SOUND UP - MANDLA QWANE

11:05 In terms of what the leadership has given us to this point , is that the anc is really struggling with finances. And that struggle can be felt, openly seen through the non payment of salaries and all these other challenges that relate to non availability of funds.
VO - Qwane is struggling to get by. Having no income is hurting his credit score, he says.
SOUND UP - MANDLA QWANE

09:20 It obviously affected our credit status. Most of us today can't get credit because we are unreliable. Unfortunately we can't even say to the bank , look I won’t be able to pay money for this money , because there is no indication that there will be payment.
VO - Qwane isn’t the only one frustrated by the ruling party’s financial woes.

Carl Niehaus has been vocal about the financial distress suffered by employees due to the party’s cash crunch. Having first been suspended as an ANC member, Niehaus has also now been fired as a Luthuli House employee.

Earlier this month, the ANC released a statement dismissing claims made by Niehaus, calling his behaviour “counter revolutionary.”

His conflict with the ANC didn’t deter him from laying criminal charges of fraud against the party on Thursday, at the Johannesburg Central Police Station.
SOUND UP - CARL NIEHAUS CLIP 0005.MXF

BONGANI 00:10 How bad are things at Luthuli House?

CARL: 00:15 I think it's bad Bongani, the mismanagement over the past few years have been shocking, the finances of the ANC, and it's not a secret, is in tatters.

BONGANI 03:35 reports have been that UIF have not been paid over, medical aid and provident fund? What do you know

03:46 I know what I see on my payslip that every month PAYE provident fund, all of those deductions have been made. But the reality is since 2018 those monies that have been deducted have not been transferred to the relevant authorities, that's a very serious matter. 4:41 So the question arises, where did the money go, because it's not in my salary. It has been taken, it was deducted, in any environment that would be considered fraud and theft.


VO - We made enquiries with the ANC over the alleged unpaid UIF and PAYE but we received no response.
VO - The ANC has repeatedly blamed the new Political Party Funding Act, or PPFA, for its financial woes.

Generally, political parties receive money in proportion to their last election result , from a fund managed by the IEC.

But the Act, which came into effect on the 1st of April, aims to make additional donations from private donors transparent.

The PPFA compels political parties to disclose all donations received above R100 000, whether in cash
or in kind. It also prohibits donations from foreign governments or organs of state.




BONGANI LINK

Chicken Braai Packs, expensive whiskey, donations from illicit tobacco - the fact is, until now political party funding has been very murky in South Africa. New legislation is aimed at changing that. But some political parties contend it's going to drive away their donors.
SOUND UP - ROBYN INTERVIEW CLIP 008.MXF

01:16 BONGANI How much has the political funding act been a game changer in our politics?


06:13 The political party funding act is a game changer for us. Its the first legislation of its kind in south africa. The first one we have had in years of democracy...it speaks to the issues we have had in the past like political party financing.


VO - Robyn Pasensie is a researcher at My Vote Counts, a non profit organisation that has for years been at the forefront of calls for the regulation of public and private funding of political parties.
She says the long-awaited Act, will go a long way in
clamping down on corruption and to lift the veil of secrecy over the funding of SA politics.
SOUND UP - ROBYN INTERVIEW CLIP 008.MXF

01:53 BONGANI : What is it going to allow that wasn't there before?

O7:15 what this act will allow is really how our political parties are financed, the sources of their donations, how they spend their money and this is really important to us because we have never had this opportunity before .
VO - The IEC’s Chief Executive for Party funding, George Mahlangu agrees. He says the Act is one of the biggest legislative changes to come into effect since the dawn of democracy.
SOUND UP - GEORGE MAHLANGU - CLIP 0001.MXF

00:34 BONGANI 0:21 How important is it for voters to know who is funding the political parties they vote for?

00:47 The political funding act is important in a sense that it seeks to promote accountability and transparency. And I think your question would be relevant on the transparency part. As voters would be in a position to know who is funding who. So that when they take decisions at a voting booth, at least they have an understanding that the political party that they are voting for, who is behind in terms of funding.
VO - Despite being lauded as a progressive necessity, some political parties are already crying foul over its unintended consequences.


BONGANI LINK

It’s not swinging open. This is the entrance to Luthuli House. The ANC headquarters. Normally it would be a hive of activity. Security guards everywhere. Officials coming in and out. And on a good day you might spot a member of the top six. It’s been erely quiet because of lockdown and COVID regulations as the party has scaled down. But it raises a question - in so much financial distress, can the ANC return to its former glory?


VO - The PPFA will most likely cause the ANC’s previously generous donors to close their wallets, says political analyst, Mcebisi Ndletyana.
SOUND UP - MCEBISI MDLETYANA CLIP 0004.MXF
01:20 Bongani: Decades into power how is it that the ANC finds itself in such a state of disarray?

Well for a number of reasons, it has to do with the administration of the various offices of the ANC at Luthuli house, provincial offices, it has to do with proper management of their own finances. 0142 and of course the state of donors whether they have a number of donors and how much they now get from the IEC

MCEBISI 39:55 Now when it comes to having to disclose and then there is a cap. If you get more than R100 000 you need to disclose where you got that money from.

BONGANI: As do the donors.

MCEBISI 40:00 As do the donors. And one donor can not donate no more than 50 million per year so a lot of ANC donors, donors generally, did not want their identity known, some of them they donate. Expecting something in return but as soon as there is a tender advertised you need to tell me and i'll submit my bid and when that donor does get that tender that's normal. 40;54 here now We are into the age of disclosure. I don't want people to know or suspect corruption and the ANC can't go to their usual donors that they would get money from.


VO - Niehaus insists the PPFA has done no one a favor - neither the ANC or any other political party.
SOUND UP - Carl NIehaus
Clip 0007.MXF
00: 09 the political party funding act has caused trouble for all political parties
Clip 006.MXF
0636 I know that the ANC relies on donors. And that in general donors are shy. Of getting their names mentioned in terms of donations.
VO - Qwane on the other hand, believes the PPFA should have been given more thought before it was passed into law .
SOUND UP - MANDLA QWANE

13:30 It was a mistake that we committed ourselves as the ANC, nobody else, it's our mistake. And we are saying part of the negotiations that we have had with the leadership of the ANC is that lets find ways to go and amend the act. If we do not and we think we will just side step it it means we will have an unsustainable approach on how we deal with this problem of finances.
SOUND UP - MCEBISI NDLETYANA CLIP0004.MXF

41:26 BONGANI If the funds dry up whether you like the ANC or not, or any other party for that matter. That can't be good for democracy either.
41:30 It can't be good for democracy. Part of the concern has always been that money tends to influence politics. So you don't want to have parties that have money being the only parties that are popular and get voted for. Because for parties to be voted for they need visibility and that comes with campaigning and that requires a lot of money.
VO - It may be too soon to judge the impact of the Political Party Funding Act on South African politics. And although some political parties are anxious about losing donors, the optimistic believe it presents opportunities for enhancement.
